sections.overview: The House Swift is a small, dark swift of South and East Asia, especially at home around towns and buildings.
sections.identification: In Japan, measured body length is about 13 cm and wingspan about 28 cm. Vietnamese adults averaged 29.6 g, with mean wing length 134.9 mm and tail length 48.1 mm. The sexes look alike. The Vietnamese mass and wing measurements pool adults and do not report a male–female split. The bird is sooty brown-black, with a pale throat, a clear white rump, long curved wings and a short, shallowly notched tail. The Little Swift, Apus affinis, is its closest evolutionary cousin and can look very similar; compare rump width, pale under-tail area and tail shape carefully. The larger Pacific Swift, Apus pacificus, has longer wings and a more deeply forked tail, while its underparts show pale scalloping absent in the House Swift. No comparable source gives a standard body width or height.
sections.habitat: It occupies open country, towns and lowland landscapes, and can breed in cliffs as well as on human structures. A Vietnamese study found most nests on older buildings, especially beneath eaves. In Japan it also nests under bridges and may reuse old Red-rumped Swallow nests. Birds forage above nearby hills, rivers and lakes.
sections.diet: It feeds on flying insects caught on the wing. A Vietnamese study found Hymenoptera, termites, beetles, bugs and flies among the main prey groups; the mix delivered to chicks differed somewhat from the adults’ diet.
sections.behavior: House Swifts often forage and nest socially, circling rapidly over settlements and open ground. Most populations are described as resident, although local seasonal movements occur; the species’ broad range does not follow one uniform migration pattern.
sections.reproduction: The nest is a small cup of light material bound with saliva, usually under a sheltered ledge. In Vietnam, two broods were usual within a 164–168 day breeding season; incubation lasted 23–30 days and young fledged after 40–48 days. Japanese observations report two or three attempts per season, so timing and output vary by region.
sections.ecology: By catching insects above urban neighborhoods and open spaces, it links nesting sites to the surrounding aerial food web.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2016 classified the species as Least Concern globally. Kyoto reports a small local breeding colony threatened by removal of old Red-rumped Swallow nests.
